newsitem.title: USA: Large U.S. chain stores post mixed September sales.
newsitem.headline: Large U.S. chain stores post mixed September sales.

text.p: Large U.S. chain stores on Thursday posted mixed September sales, although chilly fall weather has lifted business across the board in recent days and bolstered hopes for a solid holiday season.
Last month's sales were hurt by a blast of Indian summer heat and an accounting shift that left most of the Labor Day weekend out of September results this year.
Business at big discounters and several department store retailers was poor.

Federated Department Stores Inc., parent of Macy's and Bloomingdale's, Dayton Hudson Corp., which owns Marshall Field's, Dayton's and Hudson's, and May Department Stores Co., parent of Lord & Taylor, all had flat or lower sales during September.
Others recorded robust gains. Sears, Roebuck and Co., J.C. Penney Co. Inc. and specialty retailer Limited Inc had some of the biggest increases.
"September was fair," said Thomas Tashjian of Montgomery Securities. "I'd give it a C to a C plus grade. And I suspect the holiday season will come in as a B, or maybe a B plus."
A Salomon Brothers index of same-store sales, or sales at stores open at least a year, rose 3.7 percent last month compared with a 3.6 percent increase in August.

Many retailers said sales were disappointing, but they generally expect a rebound in October. Most chains should have an easy time showing year-on-year increases this month because unseasonably warm weather depressed sales in October 1995.
Dayton Hudson Chairman and Chief Executive Robert Ulrich said all three of the company's divisions were "somewhat below plan," but earnings were still on track.

"Despite the sales shortfall during the month, third-quarter profits for the company remain in line with expectations," Ulrich said in a statement. In addition to 67 department stores, Dayton Hudson owns discounter Target and Mervyn's, a moderately priced retailer.

Wall Street analysts said they had not changed their view that third-quarter earnings for the industry would increase moderately. Since retailers do not close the books on the quarter until the end of October, they will benefit from the pickup in fall apparel sales produced by the cooler weather, analysts said.

Price markdowns are not as widespread this year as last fall because stores have stocked less merchandise. While bargains are still available, the markdowns are not as steep and sweeping, leaving profits more robust, analysts said.

"Companies are focusing on profit growth," said Michael Exstein of PaineWebber. "There is not the same level of ruinous, irrational competition in the industry that began this time last year and culminated at Christmas time."

Stores that cater to teenagers showed some of the strongest gains. Anaheim, Calif.-based Pacific Sunwear Inc's sales rose 29 percent, and analysts estimate that Wet Seal Inc, parent of Contempo Casuals, had a 12 percent gain. Women's clothing chain AnnTaylor Stores Corp posted a 15.5 percent increase.

"I think the retailers are a lot wiser than in the past," said Elizabeth Pierce of Stephens Inc. "It used to be that they counted on Christmas to come along and pull them up. Now that's not always the case."
